BPM Justification: Region choice sets the carbon intensity of the electricity grid powering every process instance a BPM platform runs, and the guideline explicitly frames the decision around sustainability KPIs alongside business requirements. That is a direct, strategic sustainability lever for whatever operations, including process automation, run in that region, which is why I read it as specific rather than generic.

Dynamic scaling avoids overprovisioned, energy-hungry capacity sitting idle, a textbook sustainability win, but as described this reads as generic cloud elasticity advice rather than something argued specifically through a process lens.

Relaxing SLAs is one of the highest-leverage sustainability moves available since it reduces the always-on redundant capacity needed to meet a deadline, but whether that gets encoded into an actual process versus staying an abstract organizational target varies by case.

Decommissioning unused resources is fundamental waste-reduction practice, and 'assets' plausibly extends to retired process definitions or abandoned automation projects sitting idle, though the guideline itself is generic cloud hygiene.

Placing workloads to shorten network paths meaningfully cuts the networking resources and associated emissions of any distributed system, and could plausibly guide where distributed process tasks or engines are deployed relative to each other, though the guideline itself doesn't call that out.

This is about the physical equipment issued to team members, not the systems they use, but there's a loose connection insofar as process participants (human task performers) are among the 'team members' whose resource footprint this addresses.
Flattening demand with buffering/throttling directly reduces the peak provisioned capacity a workload needs, a genuine and fairly generic capacity-management sustainability technique.

Queue-driven, asynchronous execution keeps resources consistently utilized instead of idling, which is a real efficiency/sustainability pattern, though I can't speak to how specifically this maps onto process-orchestration terminology.

Removing dead or underused components is a meaningful waste-reduction lever, and could extend to pruning unused process branches or retired task implementations, though the guideline is written as generic software maintenance.
Optimizing hot-path code is one of the more direct levers on a workload's energy consumption, since inefficient code burns compute regardless of how well the surrounding architecture is designed.

Client-device impact (manufacturing footprint, energy use, e-waste) is a significant green-IT topic in its own right, but the tie to BPM is a stretch, at most process participants interacting with a workload through devices.

Matching software and storage patterns to actual data access needs avoids over-provisioned, energy-wasteful storage, and process-carried data (documents, variables) is one plausible instance of the data this guideline targets.

Classifying data by criticality to pick an energy-efficient storage tier is a well-established green-data-governance practice, and process-generated documents and history are a natural candidate for such classification.
Matching storage technology to access patterns is generically useful for avoiding over-provisioned storage, and applies to process data the same way it applies to any other dataset.

Automated retention and deletion policies are one of the most concrete, high-value sustainability actions for any accumulating dataset, and process instance history/audit trails accumulate continuously and indefinitely if nobody sets a policy, which makes this a clear, common case for exactly this guideline.
Storage elasticity avoids over-provisioning capacity ahead of need, a generic but real efficiency practice with no specific tie to how data is used by a process.

Removing redundant data is straightforward storage-footprint reduction, and duplicated process variables or documents accumulated across many instances are a plausible source of exactly this kind of waste.
Shared storage to avoid duplicating data is a solid, generic efficiency pattern that would reduce redundant copies of process documents the same way it reduces redundant copies of anything else.
Cutting the volume of data moved across networks reduces real networking energy use, and is a generically valuable practice regardless of what kind of workload is generating the traffic.
Skipping backups for easily-recreated data is a sound, generic storage-cost/footprint reduction; process history is one dataset this could apply to among many.
Right-sizing hardware to actual need is basic, generic efficiency practice; a process engine is simply one of many workloads that benefits.

Continually adopting more energy-efficient instance types (better performance-per-watt) is one of the clearest, most commonly-cited levers in cloud sustainability guidance, and every process worker ultimately executes on some instance type, so this reaches every process running on the platform, even though the recommendation itself is generic hardware-procurement advice.

Delegating operation to a managed service shifts efficiency responsibility to a provider who typically runs at higher utilization than a self-managed deployment would, a real but very generic cloud sustainability argument.

Optimizing use of accelerated computing hardware is a meaningful sustainability lever specifically for AI/ML-heavy workloads, and as more processes embed AI-driven decision or classification tasks, this becomes relevant to the execution of those specific tasks, though it's situational rather than universal.

Cascading sustainability targets to IT teams is exactly how those targets should end up shaping process owners' design decisions (which SLAs to relax, which region to pick), so this is a specific enabling condition for sustainability-aware process design rather than generic communication advice.

Iteratively validating and rolling out small improvements is a solid sustainability delivery practice, avoiding costly, high-footprint big-bang rollouts, and resembles continuous process improvement, though as stated it's generic agile/DevOps methodology.
Keeping software current to pick up efficiency improvements is sound, generic maintenance hygiene that applies to a process engine the same way it applies to anything else.
Increasing utilization of build/test environments is generic infrastructure efficiency, though build/test pipelines do resemble automated task sequences in a loose, structural sense.
Sharing managed device farms instead of duplicating physical test hardware is sound infrastructure-sharing efficiency, generic in nature.
